name: Chronic cor pulmonale
aliases: right heart disease from lung disease

clinicalPearls: Right ventricular enlargement and eventual failure caused by pulmonary hypertension arising from disease of the lungs, their vasculature, or the control of breathing, excluding causes originating in the left heart

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is the commonest underlying cause, followed by interstitial lung disease, chronic thromboembolic disease, and disorders of ventilation such as obesity hypoventilation and sleep-disordered breathing
Presents insidiously with exertional breathlessness and fatigue, then signs of right heart failure including raised jugular venous pressure, hepatic congestion, ascites, and peripheral oedema
Examination may reveal a left parasternal heave, a loud pulmonary component of the second heart sound, and a tricuspid regurgitant murmur
Echocardiography is central for estimating pulmonary pressures and assessing right ventricular size and function, while the primary diagnosis rests on lung assessment
The cornerstone of treatment is optimal management of the underlying lung disorder, with long-term oxygen therapy for chronic hypoxaemia being of particular prognostic value
Diuretics relieve congestion but require care to avoid reducing right ventricular filling, and pulmonary vasodilators are generally not indicated for cor pulmonale due to lung disease
reference.pathophysiology: Chronic cor pulmonale develops when a respiratory disorder raises pulmonary vascular resistance and pressure. Alveolar hypoxia causes pulmonary arteriolar vasoconstriction and, over time, vascular remodelling; loss or destruction of the pulmonary vascular bed in emphysema or fibrosis and obliteration by chronic thromboembolism add a fixed component. The right ventricle responds to this sustained afterload with hypertrophy and then dilatation, and as it fails, right atrial pressure rises and systemic venous congestion produces the characteristic oedema, hepatic congestion, and ascites. Correcting hypoxaemia can relieve the reversible vasoconstrictive element of the pulmonary hypertension.
additionalDifferentials: Left heart failure causing pulmonary venous hypertension
Right ventricular myocardial disease or infarction
Congenital heart disease with pulmonary hypertension
additionalInvestigations: Echocardiography to estimate pulmonary artery pressure and assess right ventricular size and function
Pulmonary function tests and arterial blood gas analysis to define the lung disorder and hypoxaemia
Chest imaging with radiography and CT to characterise the underlying lung and vascular disease
Ventilation-perfusion scanning or CT pulmonary angiography to detect chronic thromboembolic disease
Right heart catheterisation to confirm pulmonary hypertension and its type when management depends on it
redFlags: Progressive right heart failure with refractory oedema and hepatic congestion
Severe or worsening hypoxaemia requiring oxygen assessment
Syncope or presyncope suggesting markedly raised pulmonary pressures
Features pointing to chronic thromboembolic disease that may be surgically treatable
reference.prognosis: The outlook is largely governed by the underlying lung disease; the onset of overt right heart failure signals advanced disease and a poorer prognosis, though long-term oxygen therapy improves survival in chronically hypoxaemic patients.
pitfalls: Attributing right heart failure to lung disease without excluding left heart disease or chronic thromboembolism
Over-diuresis that lowers right ventricular preload and reduces cardiac output
Using pulmonary vasodilators intended for pulmonary arterial hypertension in cor pulmonale from lung disease, worsening gas exchange
Failing to identify and treat correctable hypoxaemia and sleep-disordered breathing
references: Braunwald's Heart Disease: A Textbook of Cardiovascular Medicine
ESC/ERS Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of pulmonary hypertension
